name: Boehm-Demers-Weiser GC (bdwgc)
workload: Author's GC benchmark (small-object allocation heavy, C variant), modified to run multiple client threads sharing one heap; elapsed seconds for the GC build versus a malloc/free variant of the same benchmark.
claimed_speedup: docs/scale.md: thread-unsafe collector 9 s vs glibc malloc/free 10.51 s (pthreads not linked), about 1.17x (derived from page data); thread-safe collector (-D GC_THREADS) 10.3 s vs glibc malloc/free 20.90 s (one thread, pthreads linked), about 2.0x (derived from page data); two clients 23.5 s vs 24.55 s, about 1.04x (derived from page data). The same page states the benchmark favors a garbage collector since most objects are small. docs/overview.md claims, without numbers, that the collector may be faster for very small objects and slower for large ones, and may significantly outperform malloc/free with thread-local allocation.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the baseline comparison (GC built with -D GC_THREADS; later table adds -D PARALLEL_MARK -D THREAD_LOCAL_ALLOC); optimization level unstated.
hardware: Dual-processor Pentium III/500, Linux 2.2.12, ancient GC release from 2000
stars_or_usage: 3.5k stars; packaged in many distributions (Repology badge in README)
tradeoffs: Conservative stack/heap scanning means false retention and no precise object layout; the docs say large-object allocation is slower than malloc and programs usually need more memory; collection pauses unless the incremental mode is used; thread-local allocation and parallel marking are build-time options; GC_MALLOC_ATOMIC and root hints are needed for best speed.
caveats: Only first-party numbers, from a roughly 25-year-old collector release on a Pentium III/500 under Linux 2.2.12 with an old glibc; compiler and flags unstated; the author says the workload favors a collector (mostly small objects). The benchmark source is hosted on the author's site (hboehm.info, not reachable from this session), so the run could not be reproduced from the repo. The single-thread figure is a modest 1.17x; the 2.0x figure compares a pthreads-linked malloc build, where glibc paid locking cost. The repo docs themselves say the collector is slower for large objects. A third-party 1992 technical report (Zorn, seen only as a search snippet) reports a trivial slowdown versus malloc/free but about twice the memory, so independent evidence points to competitive rather than faster. The license is the MIT-style permissive Boehm-GC text (SPDX Boehm-GC, not OSI-listed); a few GNU build files carry a modified GPL. The lead URL ivmai/bdwgc is the old home of this repository.

baseline: scalar POPCNT instruction loop (the __builtin_popcountll / std::popcount style baseline) and the library's own earlier Harley-Seal AVX2 path
workload: Counting 1 bits in a byte array of 96 bytes to 1 KB using a plain AVX2 popcnt256 loop instead of scalar POPCNT or Harley-Seal (libpopcnt 4.2 ChangeLog entry); the repo's benchmark program otherwise times popcnt() over fixed array sizes (23, 101, 1001, 10001, 16384 bytes in CI).
claimed_speedup: ChangeLog 4.2: 'Up to 3x faster popcount for medium arrays (96 bytes to 1 KB) using a simple AVX2 popcnt256 loop instead of scalar POPCNT or Harley-Seal.' Also 'Up to 6x faster on old x86 CPUs without POPCNT' (baseline not named) and README example of 133.5 GB/s for a 16 KB array with the AVX512 algorithm (no baseline given).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the ChangeLog claims; README says build with -O3 or -O2 and no -mavx2 needed (runtime CPUID dispatch).
hardware: ChangeLog claims: not stated. README example run: AMD EPYC 9R14 (2023), AVX512 algorithm, 16 KB array.

tradeoffs: Header-only; runtime CPUID dispatch (POPCNT, AVX2, AVX512 VPOPCNTDQ, ARM NEON, SVE, PPC64 POPCNTD, portable fallback); no special compiler flags needed; thread-safe. Only counts bits in a byte array (no bitset container).

The AVX2 Harley-Seal algorithm comes from the Mula, Kurz and Lemire paper 'Faster Population Counts using AVX2 Instructions' and the sse-popcount repository (peer-reviewed numbers for the algorithm, not opened here because arXiv is blocked and sse-popcount's README holds no tables), so the paper's numbers are not attributed to libpopcnt. Against Tensorizer: S3 4.88 s (concurrency 32) vs 37.36 s (16 workers), about 7.7x (derived); GP3 14.34 s vs 16.11 s; IO2 7.53 s vs 10.36 s; vLLM on S3 23.18 s vs 65.18 s (about 2.8x, derived).
hardware: AWS g5.12xlarge (4x NVIDIA A10G, one GPU used); GP3 SSD 750 GB, 16,000 IOPS, 1,000 MiB/s; IO2 SSD 500 GB, 100,000 IOPS, up to 4,000 MiB/s; S3 bucket in the same region. Needs libcurl and libssl; builds libstreamers3.so statically linked to libssl, libcrypto and libcurl by default. Gains depend on storage that scales with concurrency; on GP3 the win is capped by the disk's 1 GiB/s limit.

Baseline is the vLLM-bundled safetensors loader, not PyTorch torch.load; the safetensors time of 47.99 s on GP3 is almost the same as Model Streamer at concurrency 1 (47.56 s), so the win comes from parallel reads, not a faster single stream, and the safetensors loader gets one sequential cold read (roughly 0.3 GB/s from a disk that allows 1 GiB/s). Cold start was forced only by storage choice and, for S3, a two-minute wait; no cache drop command is named. Single run per cell, no variance. Tensorizer ran without optional hashing. Docs figures are images plus tables; only tables were read. A Microsoft Azure SDK blog (up to 6x with Azure Blob) and an NVIDIA developer blog were seen in search results but not opened (egress blocked or not needed).

baseline: Atlas (HP persistent-memory failure-atomic-section library) and Mnemosyne (word-level STM persistent memory); plain pthreads is faster than NVthreads
workload: Making multi-threaded programs durable on emulated NVM (tmpfs with 1000 ns delay per 4 KB page write): 14 Phoenix and PARSEC benchmarks with 12 threads against Atlas, a 4 MB-per-4-threads page-modification microbenchmark against Atlas and Mnemosyne, and PageRank (Slashdot graph and LiveJournal) against both.
claimed_speedup: EuroSys 2017 paper: 'NVthreads is 2x-10x faster than Mnemosyne and more than 2x faster than Atlas'; 'in 10 out of the 12 workloads on which Atlas ran, NVthreads is from 7% to 100x faster depending upon the workload' (NVthreads about 7% and 50% slower than Atlas on streamcluster and reverse index); microbenchmark 'NVthreads is 3x-30x faster than these systems'; PageRank on the Slashdot graph at 12 cores: 170 ms per iteration vs 500 ms Atlas (about 2.9x, derived from page data) and 5 s Mnemosyne (about 29x, derived from page data); LiveJournal: 5 s vs 29 s Atlas, 'almost 6x faster'. Against plain pthreads it is slower: 9 of 14 apps under 28% overhead, but canneal, dedup, ferret and reverse index over 4x.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper; the library's src/Makefile builds with -O3 -DNDEBUG -msse2 -fPIC.
hardware: Two Intel Xeon X5650 (12 cores at 2.67 GHz), 198 GB RAM, 600 GB SSD, Ubuntu 14.04 (Linux 3.16.7); NVM emulated with a modified tmpfs on DRAM adding 1000 ns per 4 KB page write
tradeoffs: Drop-in pthreads replacement that adds persistence: Dthreads-style multi-process execution with copy-on-write page buffering, page-granularity redo logs and recovery; overhead versus plain pthreads is 20 to 28% on easy workloads and over 4x on others; needs an NVM filesystem; research prototype ('use at your own risk'); log space 165 MB to 300 MB versus 550 MB-3.2 GB for Mnemosyne in the microbenchmark.
caveats: The baselines are other persistence systems, not std::thread or pthreads, so the guessed baseline (std::thread) does not apply and NVthreads is slower than unmodified pthreads. NVM is emulated; Atlas could not run canneal and dedup, Mnemosyne ran only the microbenchmark and a small PageRank graph (it crashes above 4 MB of durable data), and the Mnemosyne 2 s fork overhead was excluded. Compiler flags for the benchmark applications are not stated in the paper. License file is GPL-2.0 (COPYING) while the awesome-cpp listing says LGPL-2.1, and the tree vendors Atlas, Mnemosyne and Dthreads code under their own licenses. Category thread-pools-work-stealing is the closest fit among wave-11 categories; the project is really persistent-memory threading.
